And low power does worse than miss. Test a real effect of point three with fifteen per group, and only twelve percent of runs reach significance. Those winners average point eight five, nearly three times the truth. Only the runs that noise exaggerated made it through. Every test in those simulations was a t-test.

Its statistic is a ratio: the gap you observed, over the noise in that gap, its standard error. A big t means the gap dwarfs the noise. A small one means it's the size of an ordinary wobble. It comes in three designs: one group against a target, two separate groups, or the same units measured twice.

That last one matters more than it looks. Twenty-five patients' blood pressure, before and after a program. Compare the two columns as separate groups, and the differences between people drown the change. p is point one one five. Test each patient's own change instead, and the noise collapses. t is ten, and p is under one in a billion. Same data. Each patient just became their own control. With more than two groups, the tempting move is a t-test for every pair.

Five groups make ten pairs. Draw all five from the same process, and some pair comes up significant in thirty-two percent of trials. That's the many-looks problem again. ANOVA asks once: do any of the means differ? Its F statistic is the spread between the group means, over the spread within the groups. Three warehouses' delivery times give an F of twelve. At least one of them differs... but ANOVA won't say which.
